newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: No new law for Dutch shareholder say - committee.
newsitem.headline: No new law for Dutch shareholder say - committee.

text.p: A raft of 40 recommendations aimed at improving corporate governance and increasing shareholder say at Dutch listed companies unveiled on Wednesday need not be backed by new legislation, compilers said.

Presenting his final report, chairman Jaap Peters of the Committee on Corporate Governance told a news conference: "We believe that existing legislation together with our recommendations will be sufficient to achieve an improvement."
Given the diversity of rulings governing Dutch companies, legislation to enforce the recommendations would be well-nigh impossible, he added.

The committee, appointed last year by the Amsterdam Stock Exchange Association and listed companies' organisation VEUO, has been looking into ways to improve corporate transparency and give capital providers more say.
Its institution reflects the mounting pressure on Dutch companies in recent years to dismantle anti-takeover constructions and give shareholders a say more in keeping with their financial stake.
The report's recommendations cover the composition and functioning of Dutch management and supervisory boards and executive remuneration.
Under the proposals, companies should publish details of stock options given to members of management and supervisory boards and other staff, along with the most significant conditions attached.

To date Dutch listed companies have not been required to publish such details, but recent media revelations of generous stock option schemes enjoyed by corporate executives have sparked public indignation.

In the area of shareholder say, the committee recommends that shareholders with investments above a specified threshold should be allowed to put forward points for the agenda of the annual general meeting of shareholders (AGM).

In addition a company should justify the issue of financial preference shares at a prior meeting of shareholders, the report recommends, adding the issue of preference shares as a protective device is deemed undesirable.
The report further recommends the introduction of proxy solicitation rights aimed at enhancing shareholder involvement in decision making at the AGM.
However, critics have been quick to point out that no provision has been made for enforcing the committee's recommendations.
Companies are expected to implement the bulk of the measures and give their reasons for the non-implementation of others in their 1998 annual reports.
In the latter half of next year, Peters, a former chairman of Dutch insurer Aegon, will head a follow-up committee of three to monitor corporate compliance with the recommendations.
But the one-off monitoring will do no more than publicly register the extent of each company's compliance, Peters said.
Shareholders' lobby group VEB said on Wednesday it would continue to press for legislation if corporate compliance with the measures proved disappointing.
"The VEB clearly supports the recommendations put forward by the committee...but I do ask whether these will be sufficient," VEB chairman Peter Paul de Vries said in an initial reaction.
He said the VEB was particularly concerned that Dutch companies implemented the measures aimed at enhancing shareholder say.
"I would have liked it very much if the bourse were to refuse as members companies which would not meet a certain number of minimum requirements," De Vries said.
For example, the Amsterdam bourse could refuse listings to companies which issued share receipts without voting rights, he noted.
But AEX chairman George Moeller said that in the current open economy of internationally operating companies, the Amsterdam bourse could not unilaterally change its listings requirements.
